indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.1.2 Show understanding of the roles of condensation, evaporation, transpiration and precipitation in the hydrological (water) cycle
indicator.objective: Explain how rain falls from clouds

skills.description: Define evaporation, condensation, dew point, ice, cloud, gravity and precipitation.
Explain simply how clouds are formed (water vapour cools and condenses around dust particles).
Explain how raindrops form around tiny dust or smoke particles and grow heavy.
Explain that gravity causes the raindrops to fall from the clouds.
Recognise that not all clouds produce rain.
Link rain formation to the water cycle (evaporation → condensation → precipitation).

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions total — Difficulty 1: 5; Difficulty 2: 7; Difficulty 3: 5; Difficulty 4: 3.
misconceptions: Rain falls directly from the sun.
Evaporation and condensation are the same.
Rain falls because clouds are heavy with air only.

questions.stem: What is evaporation?
options: Water changing from liquid to vapour
Water changing from vapour to liquid
questions.explanation: Evaporation is the change of water from liquid to vapour.
questions.misconception: Evaporation is the same as condensation.

questions.stem: What is condensation?
options: Water vapour changing into liquid droplets
hints: Think about droplets on a cold glass.
questions.explanation: Condensation is the change of water vapour into liquid droplets when it cools.
questions.misconception: Condensation is the same as evaporation.

questions.stem: What is precipitation?
answer: water falling from clouds as rain, snow, or hail
questions.explanation: Precipitation is water falling from clouds as rain, snow, or hail.
questions.misconception: Precipitation is when water evaporates.

questions.stem: How are clouds formed?
options: Water vapour cools and condenses around dust particles
Rain falls upwards to form clouds
Wind blows clouds from the ground
questions.explanation: Clouds are formed when water vapour rises, cools and condenses around tiny dust particles in the air.
questions.misconception: Clouds are made by the sun directly.

questions.stem: What happens to water vapour when it rises and cools?
options: It condenses into tiny water droplets
questions.explanation: When water vapour rises and cools, it condenses into tiny water droplets that form clouds.
questions.misconception: Water vapour disappears in the sky.

questions.stem: Explain how clouds are formed.
answer: water vapour rises, cools and condenses around dust particles
water vapour cools and condenses into droplets
vapour rises and condenses to form clouds
questions.explanation: Clouds form when water vapour rises, cools and condenses around tiny dust particles in the air.
questions.misconception: Clouds are made by the sun.

questions.stem: Why do clouds form high in the sky?
options: Because water vapour rises and cools at higher altitudes
Because the sun pushes clouds up
Because clouds are lighter than air
hints: It cools as it goes higher.
questions.explanation: Clouds form high in the sky because water vapour rises with warm air and cools at higher altitudes, where it condenses into droplets.
questions.misconception: Clouds form because they are light.

questions.stem: How do raindrops form in clouds?
options: Tiny water droplets join together around dust particles and grow bigger
Wind blows raindrops from the ground
questions.explanation: Raindrops form when tiny water droplets in clouds join together around dust particles and grow bigger and heavier.
questions.misconception: Raindrops form from nothing.

questions.stem: What happens to water droplets in a cloud when they become too heavy?
questions.explanation: When water droplets in a cloud become too heavy, they fall as rain.
questions.misconception: Heavy droplets rise higher.

questions.stem: Explain how raindrops form and grow in clouds.
answer: tiny water droplets join together around dust particles and grow bigger until they are heavy enough to fall
water droplets combine and grow around dust particles
droplets join and grow until they fall as rain
questions.explanation: Tiny water droplets in clouds join together around dust particles. As they combine, they grow bigger and heavier until they fall as rain.
questions.misconception: Raindrops form from nothing.

questions.stem: Why do raindrops need tiny dust or smoke particles to form?
options: Water vapour condenses more easily around these particles
Dust particles are made of water
Dust particles push the rain down
hints: Vapour needs a surface to condense on.
questions.explanation: Water vapour condenses more easily around tiny dust or smoke particles, which act as surfaces for droplets to form on.
questions.misconception: Dust particles are made of water.

questions.stem: What causes raindrops to fall from clouds?
hints: Things fall down due to this force.
It pulls objects towards the earth.
questions.explanation: Gravity causes raindrops to fall from clouds to the ground.
questions.misconception: Gravity pushes raindrops up.

questions.stem: What force causes rain to fall from clouds?
hints: It is the same force that makes objects fall.
questions.explanation: Gravity is the force that causes rain to fall from clouds.
questions.misconception: Wind causes rain to fall.

questions.stem: A learner says, 'Rain falls because clouds push the water down.' What is the best correction?
options: Yes, clouds push the water down
No, gravity pulls the raindrops down
No, the sun pushes the rain down
No, wind pushes the rain down
questions.explanation: Rain falls because gravity pulls the raindrops down, not because clouds push them.
questions.misconception: Clouds push the rain down.

questions.stem: Do all clouds produce rain?
options: No, not all clouds produce rain
hints: Some clouds are thin and wispy.
Not every cloud has enough water to rain.
questions.explanation: Not all clouds produce rain. Some clouds do not contain enough water droplets to fall as rain.
questions.misconception: All clouds produce rain.

questions.stem: Why do some clouds not produce rain?
answer: they do not contain enough water droplets to fall as rain
the droplets are too small or light
they do not have enough water
hints: Clouds need enough water to rain.
questions.explanation: Some clouds do not produce rain because they do not contain enough water droplets to become heavy enough to fall.
questions.misconception: All clouds produce rain.

questions.stem: Which of these best explains why some clouds do not produce rain?
options: They do not contain enough water droplets to fall
They are too high in the sky
hints: If droplets are few, no rain falls.
questions.explanation: Some clouds do not produce rain because they do not contain enough water droplets to fall as rain.
questions.misconception: All clouds produce rain.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes part of the water cycle?
questions.explanation: The water cycle includes evaporation, then condensation, then precipitation (rain).
questions.misconception: The water cycle has a different order.

questions.stem: Explain how evaporation and condensation lead to rain in the water cycle.
answer: water evaporates, rises, cools and condenses into clouds, then falls as rain
evaporation puts vapour in the air, condensation forms clouds, and rain falls from clouds
water vapour rises, condenses into clouds, and then falls as rain
questions.explanation: Water evaporates into the air, rises, cools and condenses into clouds. The water droplets in clouds fall as rain.
questions.misconception: Rain falls directly from the sun.

questions.stem: Design a simple diagram showing how rain falls from clouds. Label the sun, evaporation, condensation (cloud formation), precipitation (rain), and gravity. Use arrows to show the direction of movement.

criteria.description: Showed the sun and evaporation from a water source
Showed water vapour rising and condensing into a cloud
Showed rain falling from the cloud
Labeled gravity as the force pulling the rain down
Used arrows to show direction of movement

hints: Start with the sun heating water.
Show vapour rising and forming a cloud.
questions.explanation: This is a drawing task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: Rain falls directly from the sun.
